title: Universal Inductive Inference of Quantum States
authors: Taiga Hiroka, Min-Hsiu Hsieh, Yuki Shirakawa
abstract: Solomonoff's universal inductive inference [Inf. Control. 1964] is one of the most general frameworks for learning from sequential data and predicting future observations. It provides prediction guarantees for any computable stochastic source. We ask whether an analogous universal theory of induction can be developed for quantum systems. To this end, we introduce universal quantum inductive inference, a framework for learning and predicting quantum sources that may exhibit arbitrary correlations and entanglement across time. Given the outcomes of past measurements and the corresponding post-measurement quantum systems, the learner produces a joint state that predicts the next measurement outcome and post-measurement system while preserving correlations with the past systems. We model a quantum source as a multipartite quantum state whose description is generated by an unknown $s$-bit program within a given time bound. The learner is required to produce a state that is $ε$-close in trace distance to the target with probability at least $1-δ$. We establish an information-theoretic inference algorithm with round complexity $O(sε^{-2}δ^{-1})$. We further prove a matching lower bound in the relevant parameter regime, even for classical sources. As a second result, we construct a non-i.i.d. state tomography algorithm that outputs a classical description of the conditional state of the next system given past measurement outcomes. Our information-theoretic tomography algorithm achieves round complexity $O(s\min\{2^s,2^n\}ε^{-2}δ^{-1})$, where $n$ is the number of qubits received in each round. Finally, we investigate the computational hardness of universal quantum inductive inference under quantum cryptographic assumptions.
summary: This paper extends Solomonoff's universal induction principle to the quantum domain, creating a framework for predicting future quantum states based on measurement history. It establishes efficient algorithmic bounds for this inference task and proves that these bounds are fundamentally limited by information-theoretic lower bounds. The results are significant for understanding the computational complexity of quantum state reconstruction and prediction.
main_problem: The paper develops a universal quantum inductive inference framework analogous to Solomonoff's induction for learning and predicting quantum sources.
main_result: It establishes an information-theoretic algorithm for quantum inductive inference with round complexity $O(s\epsilon^{-2}\delta^{-1})$, matching a proven lower bound.
method: The authors use information-theoretic techniques to derive both upper bounds (algorithms) and lower bounds (complexity requirements) for the inference task.
model_or_system: The system models a quantum source generating multipartite quantum states ($ho_{R_1...R_m}$) whose description is governed by an unknown $s$-bit program. The learning process involves predicting the next state and outcome given a history of measurements.
key_observables: Trace distance ($\epsilon$), round complexity, and the joint state ($\sigma_{R_1...R_iX_i}$) predicting the next outcome.
important_parameters: Source description length ($s$), error tolerance ($\epsilon$), failure probability ($\delta$), and the number of qubits ($n$).
main_assumptions: The source is assumed to be generated by an unknown $s$-bit program, and the analysis relies on quantum cryptographic assumptions for hardness results.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the inputs (past history, next instrument, conditional state) and the output (joint predicted state) of the quantum inductive learner $L$ at any given round $i$.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the quantum inductive inference problem, then presents the algorithmic solution (Theorem 1.1) and the tomography algorithm (Theorem 1.2). It follows this by proving the matching lower bounds (Theorems A.1/4) and concluding with hardness results based on one-way puzzles.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental theoretical tools for characterizing the limits of prediction and learning in quantum systems, which is crucial for quantum machine learning and quantum process tomography.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Inputs and output of the learner L at round i. The instruments I1, . . . , Ii−1 and their outcomes x1, . . . , xi−1 form the classical history h<i = (I1, x1, ..., Ii−1, xi−1). The learner receives h<i, the description of the target measurement Ii, and a single copy of the conditional post-measurement state ρR1...Ri−1|h<i. It outputs a joint state σ on R1...RiXi, where Xi stores the next measurement outcome and Ri is the next post-measurement quantum system. The output must approximate the corresponding joint state of the source conditioned on h<i, including its correlations with the past systems.
